Tolerance is derived from what you have logged, so it appears once there is something in the journal to derive it from.
These are logged, and the model has no pharmacokinetics to score them with. Listed rather than left out, so an absent card is never mistaken for a rested one.

Each dose is turned into a concentration over time at every receptor it engages. Those drive four layers that build and recover on their own clocks — within a session, over days, over months, and for the serotonin releasers a slow synthesis pool that waits weeks. The shift is what those add up to: how much further right the dose-response curve has moved.
With these layers this class does not come back toward baseline on its own.
Back within 5%% of baseline in about %1$s, if nothing else is taken.
The high has faded more than the cardiovascular load. A redose lands on a system that has not adapted with it.
Sedation has faded further than memory and coordination, which is how the dose rises while the impairment does not.
Dependence builds on its own clock, separately from how strong the effect feels.
Tolerance to the effect fades faster than the body\'s protection against it.
The effect has faded faster than the breathing protection. After a break the old dose is not as safe as it used to feel.
The cumulative-load axis runs separately from how strong the effect feels.
Read from your own log. Each class moves on its own clock, so two substances taken together do not fade together.

A level only means something with its draw time: for cypionate and enanthate, measure midway between injections; for undecanoate, measure at trough, just before the next dose.
Note the time since your last injection when you draw — a peak and a trough tell different stories, and the curve reads both against your dose times.
